findings.title: Visual pass/fail with no contrast, text or mute baseline
findings.basis: The brief judges by looks and names no contrast, text-instruction or mute baseline; WCAG 1.4.3 (4.5:1) is a reference only, no legal duty for a class project.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: WCAG is a guideline here, not a legal duty; nothing is breached.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No one is harmed by a missing baseline in a class game.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: The game still runs; legibility is a quality matter.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: Not shown for this finding.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: Not shown for this finding.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: Judges are peers rating looks; a missing contrast baseline is a gap, not a rejectable flaw.

answers.q: Is it operational friction, weaker maintainability, or minor inefficiency?
answers.why: Cheap-to-fix legibility and polish gap.

findings.underlying_problem: Make the game legible on a judge's screen and sound-off setup, with an explicit self-chosen baseline.
findings.build_consequence: Adopt a self-set baseline: 4.5:1 text contrast, instructions as on-screen text, a mute toggle, and a sound-off playthrough check before Friday.
findings.would_settle: Owner-adopted or default baseline plus a contrast check of the final UI

findings.title: Audio and colour carry game information with no second channel
findings.basis: Position, hazards and pickups may be signalled by colour or audio alone; WCAG 1.4.1/1.4.2 apply only by analogy and are not a duty here.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: WCAG is a guideline here, not a legal duty.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No harm; a free class game.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: Judges on muted laptops or with colour-vision differences lose some cues but the game still works.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: Not shown for this finding.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: Not shown for this finding.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: Design weakness, but not one a reviewer would reject a class project for.

answers.q: Is it operational friction, weaker maintainability, or minor inefficiency?
answers.why: Missing second channel for cues is a polish/usability gap.

findings.underlying_problem: Give every gameplay-critical cue a second channel so the game works muted and without relying on hue.
findings.build_consequence: Pair each sound cue with a visual cue, use shape/icon plus colour for hazards and boosts, provide a mute control, and do not autoplay audio before a user gesture.
findings.would_settle: Playthrough with sound off and with a greyscale filter

findings.title: Input method and device support unspecified for judges
findings.basis: The brief says any browser on unknown devices but never states keyboard, touch or gamepad support; WCAG 2.1.1 applicability to steering is unclear and is a guideline only.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: No law or licence is at stake; WCAG is not a duty here.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No harm.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: A failure on a judge's device is possible but not shown; devices are unknown.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: No security issue.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: No financial or legal exposure.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: A multiplayer game with unspecified input methods and no mouse-free lobby is an unstated requirement a reviewer would flag.

findings.underlying_problem: State which input methods the judging setup must support and make the lobby and steering work on them.
findings.build_consequence: Support keyboard steering and a keyboard-operable lobby by default; add touch only if the owner confirms judges use phones.
findings.owner_question: Which devices and input methods will judges use on Friday? Options: (a) laptop keyboard only; (b) laptop plus touch/phone; (c) unknown, so support keyboard and touch.
findings.would_settle: Owner states the judges' devices and input methods

findings.title: API keys or prompts could be committed to the public repo
findings.basis: The repo is public and AI agents do much of the build, so generator credentials could be committed; GitLab push protection is Ultimate-tier and may be unavailable on the instance. Remedy is rotation, not history rewrite.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: The brief does not require committing secrets.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No harm to third parties.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: No failure under implied conditions.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: A leaked generator key is not a key-recovery, RCE or privilege-escalation hole.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: Class-project keys are typically free-tier or capped; no substantial unbounded exposure shown.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: A public repo built with agents and no secret hygiene or scanning is a process flaw a reviewer would reject.

findings.underlying_problem: Keep credentials and unreleased prompts out of a public repo and be able to detect and recover if one leaks.
findings.build_consequence: Keep keys in env files that are gitignored, commit an .env.example only, add a pre-commit secret scan, tell agents never to write keys to files, and rotate any key that is ever committed.
findings.would_settle: Admin answer on instance secret-detection features; a clean scan of the first push

findings.title: Load-testing the free hosts is not authorised
findings.basis: Vercel allows load tests only on Enterprise with notice; Render prohibits DoS testing; Cloudflare permits benchmarking. A breach could get the account suspended just before judging, but it bites only if someone load-tests.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: The brief does not require load testing, so following it breaks no host terms.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No harm.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: A suspension just before judging would be damaging, but only if a load test is run; it is avoidable and not implied by the brief.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: No security hole.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: No spend or contract exposure on free tiers.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: An omitted scoping note, not a design flaw.

answers.q: Is it operational friction, weaker maintainability, or minor inefficiency?
answers.why: Operational care point: choose a test method that does not breach host policy.

findings.underlying_problem: Validate multiplayer capacity without breaching the chosen host's load-testing policy.
findings.build_consequence: Load-test only locally or against a self-run instance; on the host use a small multi-client smoke test, and read the host's terms before any heavier test.
findings.would_settle: Read Cloudflare Service-Specific Terms and the Render/Vercel policy for the chosen host

findings.title: Decoded audio held as PCM in RAM (narrowed to implementation advice)
findings.basis: Narrowed claim: decodeAudioData yields memory-resident float32 PCM meant for clips under about 45 s; a long music track is better streamed through an audio element. Applies only to C-105; autoplay unlock is unevidenced and dropped.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written plainly break a law, a licence, third-party terms of service, or professional ethics?
answers.why: Nothing breached.

answers.q: Would following the brief as written harm users or third parties, or compromise physical safety?
answers.why: No harm.

answers.q: Would the deliverable fail under the production conditions the brief itself implies (load, faults, adversaries, scale)?
answers.why: One long track is about 64 MB, fine on a judge's laptop; no documented limit was found.

answers.q: Would it open a severe security hole (key recovery, remote code execution, supply-chain compromise, privilege escalation, data exfiltration)?
answers.why: No security issue.

answers.q: Would it create substantial financial or legal exposure short of a plain breach (unit economics that cannot work, unbounded spend, contractual risk)?
answers.why: No exposure.

answers.q: Is it a correctness, measurement, statistical or design flaw that a principal-level reviewer would reject?
answers.why: Not a brief flaw; the skeptic found it is implementation advice.

answers.q: Is it operational friction, weaker maintainability, or minor inefficiency?
answers.why: Minor memory-efficiency point with an easy alternative.

findings.underlying_problem: Keep audio memory modest by decoding only short effects and streaming or looping long music.
findings.build_consequence: Decode only short SFX with Web Audio; play music through an audio element (MediaElementAudioSourceNode) or a short mono loop.
findings.would_settle: Computed decoded size of the final audio set
